readings.c1s2:
¶
'''barebacked''' (bãr′bakt), ''a.'' Having the back uncovered; unsaddled, as a horse.

'''barebind''', ''n.'' See ''bearbine''.

'''barebone''' (bãr′bōn), ''n.'' A very lean person. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|Here comes lean Jack, here comes ''bare-bone''.
{{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., ii. 4.}}}}

'''bareboned''' (bãr′bōnd), ''a.'' Having the bones bare or scantily covered with flesh; so lean that the bones show their forms.
{{smaller block|<poem>But now that fair fresh mirror, dim and old,
Shows me a ''bareboned'' death by time outworn.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1761.}}}}

'''barefaced''' (bãr′fāst), ''a.'' '''1.''' With the face uncovered; not masked.
{{smaller block|Then you will play ''bare-faced''. ''Shak.'', M. N. D., i. 2.}}
'''2.''' Undisguised; unreserved; without concealment; open: in a good or an indifferent sense. [Obsolete or archaic in this use.]
{{smaller block|It [Christianity] did not peep in dark corners, . . . but with a ''barefaced'' confidence it openly proclaimed itself.
{{right|''Barrow'', Works, II. 418.}}}}
'''3.''' Undisguised or open, in a bad sense; hence, shameless; impudent; audacious: as, a ''barefaced'' falsehood.
{{smaller block|See the ''barefaced'' villain, how he cheats, lies, perjures, robs, murders! ''Sterne'', Tristram Shandy, ii. 17.

A wretch, . . . guilty of . . . ''barefaced'' inconstancy.
{{right|''Goldsmith'', Citizen of the World, xviii.}}}}

'''barefacedly''' (bãr′fāst-li), ''adv.'' In a barefaced manner; without disguise or reserve; openly; shamelessly; impudently.
{{smaller block|Some profligate wretches own it too ''barefacedly''. ''Locke.''

''Barefacedly'' unjust. ''Carlyle'', Fred. the Gt., IV. xii. 11.}}
readings.c2s3:
¶
'''baresark''' (bãr′särk), ''adv.'' In a shirt only; without armor.
{{smaller block|I will go ''baresark'' to-morrow to the war.
{{right|''Kingsley'', Hereward, p. 169.}}}}

'''baresthesiometer''' (bar-es-thē-si-om′e-tėr), ''n.'' [< Gr. βάρος, weight, + αἴσθησις, perception, + μέτρον, measure.] An instrument for testing the sense of pressure. Also spelled ''baræsthesiometer''.

'''baret''', ''n.'' See ''barret''<sup>2</sup>.

'''bare-worn''' (bãr′wōrn), ''a.'' Worn bare; naked: as, “the ''bare-worn'' common,” ''Goldsmith'', Des. Vil.

'''barf''' (bärf), ''n.'' Same as ''bargh''.

'''bar-fee''' (bär′fē), ''n.'' In ''English law'', a fee of 20 pence, which every prisoner acquitted (at the bar) of felony formerly paid to the jailer.

'''bar-fish''' (bär′fish), ''n.'' Same as ''calico-bass''.

'''bar-frame''' (bär′frām), ''n.'' The frame supporting the ends of the grate-bars in furnaces.

'''barful''' (bär′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''bar''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ful''.] Full of obstructions or impediments. [Rare.]
{{smaller block|<poem>I’ll do my best
To woo your lady: [''Aside''] yet, a ''barful'' strife!
Whoe’er I woo, myself would be his wife.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', T. N., i. 4.}}}}

'''bargain''' (bär′gạ̄n), ''n.'' [< ME. ''bargain'', ''bargayne'', ''bargeyn'', ''bargen'', etc., < OF. ''bargaine'', ''bargaigne'' = Pr. ''barganh'', ''barganha'' = Pg. ''bar-''

''bera''), make bare, < ''bær'', bare: see ''bare''1, ''a.'']   '''1.''' To make bare; uncover; divest of covering: as, to ''bare'' one’s head or one’s breast. {{smaller block|He ''bared'' an ancient oak of all her boughs. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}} {{smaller block|That cry . . . that seemed to ''bare'' A wretched life of every softening veil. {{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 159.}}}} '''2.''' To disclose; make manifest; lay bare: as, to ''bare'' the secrets of the grave. [Archaic.] '''bare'''2 (bãr). Old preterit of ''bear''1. '''Barea''' (bā′rē-ä̤), ''n. pl.''   [Gr., neut. pl. of βαρύς, βαρέα, heavy.]   An Aristotelian group of birds, corresponding to the Linnean ''Gallinæ'', including the gallinaceous or rasorial birds. '''bareback''' (bãr′bak), ''a.'' and ''adv.'' '''I.''' ''a.'' Using or performing on a barebacked horse: as, a ''bareback'' rider. '''II.''' ''adv.'' On a barebacked horse: as, to ride ''bareback''. '''barefit''' (bãr′fit), ''a.'' Barefoot or barefooted. [Scotch.] '''barefoot''' (bãr′fu̇t), ''a.'' and ''adv.''   [< ME. ''barefote'', ''barfot'', < AS. ''bærfōt'' (= OFries. ''berfōt'' = D. ''barrevoet'' = Icel. ''berfættr''), < ''bær'', bare, + ''fōt'', foot.]   '''I.''' ''a.'' Having the feet bare; without shoes and stockings. {{smaller block|Going to find a ''barefoot'' brother out,
One of our order. {{right|''Shak.'', R. and J., v. 2.}}}} {{smaller block|Blessings on thee, little man,
''Barefoot'' boy, with cheek of tan! {{right|''Whittier'', Barefoot Boy.}}}} '''II.''' ''adv.'' With the feet bare. {{smaller block|I must dance ''barefoot.'' {{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., ii. 1.}}}} '''barefooted''' (bãr′fu̇t-ed), ''a.''   [< ''barefoot'' + ''-ed''1.]   Having the feet bare.—'''Barefooted Augustinians.''' {{smaller|See ''Augustinian.''}}—'''Barefooted Carmelites.''' {{smaller|See ''Carmelite.''}} '''barege''' (ba-räzh′), ''n.''   [< F. ''barège'', so called from ''Barèges'', a watering-place in the Pyrenees. See def.]   A thin gauze-like fabric for women’s dresses, usually made of silk and worsted, but, in the inferior sorts, with cotton in place of silk. {{smaller block|In reality bareges were never made in the village from which they have their name, the seat of the manufacture being at Bagnères-de-Bigorre in the Pyrenees.}} '''baregin, baregine''' (ba-rā′zhin), ''n.''   [< ''Barèges'' (see ''barege''), the springs of which yield the substance, + ''-in''2.]   A transparent, gelatinous, mucus-like substance, the product of certain algæ growing in thermal sulphur-springs, to which they impart the flavor and odor of flesh-broth. {{smaller|Baregin is itself odorless and tasteless. It contains, when dry, from 30 to 80 per cent. of mineral matter, chiefly silica. The organic matter contains no sulphur and from 9 to 12 per cent. of nitrogen.}} '''bare-gnawn†''' (bãr′nân), ''a.'' Gnawed or eaten bare.   ''Shak.'', Lear, v. 3. '''barehanded''' (bãr′han″ded), ''a.'' '''1.''' With uncovered hands.—'''2.''' Destitute of means; with no aid but one’s own hands: as, he began life ''barehanded''. '''bareheaded''' (bãr′hed″ed), ''a.'' Having the head uncovered, especially as a token of respect. {{smaller block|First, you shall swear never to name my lord, Or hear him nam’d hereafter, but ''bare-headed.'' {{right|''Fletcher'' (''and another''?), Queen of Corinth, iv. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|On being first brought before the court, Ridley stood ''bareheaded.'' {{right|''Froude'', Hist. Eng., xxxiii.}}}} '''bareheadedness''' (bãr′hed″ed-nes), ''n.'' The state of being bareheaded. {{smaller block|''Bareheadedness'' was in Corinth, as also in all Greece and Rome, a token of honour and superiority. {{right|''Bp. Hall'', Remains, p. 237.}}}} '''barely''' (bãr′li), ''adv.''   [< ''bare''1 + ''-ly''2.]   '''1.''' Nakedly; openly; without disguise or concealment.—'''2.''' Scantily; poorly: as, a man ''barely'' clad, or a room ''barely'' furnished.—'''3.''' Only just; no more than; with nothing over or to spare: as, she is ''barely'' sixteen. {{smaller block|In paying his debts a man ''barely'' does his duty. {{right|''Goldsmith'', The Bee, No. 3.}}}} {{smaller block|Fox himself ''barely'' succeeded in retaining his seat for Westminster. {{right|''Lecky'', Eng. in 18th Cent., xv.}}}} '''4.''' Merely; only. [Archaic.] {{smaller block|It is not ''barely'' a man’s abridgment in his external accommodations which makes him miserable. {{right|''South.''}}}} '''bareman†''' (bãr′man), ''n.''   [Sc., also ''bairman''; < ''bare''1 + ''man.'']   A bankrupt. [Scotch.] '''bareness''' (bãr′nes), ''n.'' The state of being bare. {{smaller|(''a'') Want or deficiency of clothing or covering; nakedness. (''b'') Deficiency of appropriate covering, equipment, furniture, ornament, etc.: as, “old December’s ''bareness,''” ''Shak.'', Sonnets, xcvii.}} {{smaller block|To make old ''bareness'' picturesque, And tuft with grass a feudal tower. {{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, cxxviii.}}}} {{smaller|(''c'') Leanness. [Rare.] (''d'') Poverty; indigence.}} {{smaller block|Stript of . . . its Priveleges, and made like the primitive Church for its ''Bareness.'' {{right|''South'', Sermons, I. 229.}}}} '''bare-picked''' (bãr′pikt), ''a.'' Picked bare; stripped of all flesh, as a bone. {{smaller block|The ''bare-picked'' bone of majesty. {{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iv. 3.}}}} '''bare-pump''' (bãr′pump), ''n.'' A pump for drawing liquor from a cask: used in vinegar-works, wine- and beer-cellars, in sampling, etc. Also called ''bar-pump.'' '''bare-ribbed''' (bãr′ribd), ''a.'' '''barful''' (bär′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ''bar''1 + ''-ful''.]   Full of obstructions or impediments. [Rare.] {{smaller block|I’ll do my best To woo your lady: [''Aside''] yet, a ''barful'' strife! Whoe’er I woo, myself would be his wife. {{right|''Shak.'', T. N., i. 4.}}}} '''bargain''' (bär′gạ̄n), ''n.''   [< ME. ''bargain'', ''bargayne'', ''bargeyn'', ''bargen'', etc., < OF. ''bargaine'', ''bargaigne'' = Pr. ''barganh'', ''barganha'' = Pg. ''barganha'' = It. ''bargagna'' (Pr. also ''barganh'' = It. ''bargagno''), < ML. *''barcania'', *''barcanium'', a bargain, traffic; cf. ''bargain'', ''v.'' Origin unknown; supposed by Diez and others to be from ML. ''barca'', a boat, bark, or barge, but evidence is wanting.]   '''1†.''' The act of discussing the terms of a proposed agreement; bargaining. {{smaller block|I’ll give thrice so much land To any well-deserving friend; But in the way of ''bargain'', mark ye me, I’ll cavil on the ninth part of a hair. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. IV., iii. 1.}}}} '''2†.''' A contention or contest for the mastery or upper hand; a struggle. {{smaller block|On Brudus side the better of that bloudie ''bargaine'' went. {{right|''Warner'', Albion’s Eng., XIV. xc. 365. (''N. E. D.'')}}}} '''3.''' A contract or an agreement between two or more parties; a compact settling that something shall be done; specifically, a contract by which one party binds himself to transfer the right to some property for a consideration, and the other party binds himself to receive the property and pay the consideration. {{smaller block|To clap this royal ''bargain'' up of peace. {{right|''Shak.'', K. John, iii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|''Ros.'' But if you do refuse to marry me, You’ll give yourself to this most faithful shepherd? ''Phe.'' So is the ''bargain''. {{right|''Shak.'', As you Like it, v. 4.}}}} {{smaller block|“Our fathers,” said one orator, “sold their king for southern gold, and we still lie under the reproach of that foul ''bargain''.” {{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vi.}}}} '''4.''' The outcome of an agreement as regards one of the parties; that which is acquired by bargaining; the thing purchased or stipulated for: as, look at my ''bargain''; a bad ''bargain''; “a losing ''bargain,''” ''Junius'', Letters, v. {{smaller block|She was too fond of her most filthy ''bargain.'' {{right|''Shak.'', Othello, v. 2.}}}} '''5.''' Something bought or sold at a low price; an advantageous purchase. {{smaller block|If you have a taste for paintings, egad, you shall have ’em a ''bargain.'' {{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, iii. 3.}}}} {{smaller|'''Bargain and sale''', or, more fully, ''deed of bargain and sale'', in ''law'', the form of deed now in common use for the conveyance of land: so called because it is expressed as a sale for a pecuniary consideration agreed on, being thus distinguished on the one hand from a quitclaim, which is a release, and on the other hand from the old conveyance by covenant to stand seized to uses.—'''Dutch''' or '''wet bargain,''' a bargain sealed by the parties drinking over it.—'''Into the bargain,''' over and above what is stipulated; moreover; besides.}} {{smaller block|Faith, Charles, this is the most convenient thing you could have found for the business, for ’twill serve not only as a hammer, but a catalogue ''into the bargain.'' {{right|''Sheridan'', School for Scandal, iv. 1.}}}} {{smaller|'''To beat a bargain,''' to bargain; haggle.—'''To buy at a bargain,''' to buy cheaply.—'''To buy the bargain dear†,''' to pay dearly for a thing.—'''To make the best of a bad bargain,''' to do the best one can in untoward circumstances.}} {{smaller block|I am sorry for thy misfortune; however, we must ''make the best of a bad bargain.'' {{right|''Arbuthnot'', Hist. of John Bull.}}}} {{smaller|'''To sell a bargain†,''' to entrap one into asking innocent questions, so as to give an unexpected answer, usually a coarse or indelicate one.}} {{smaller block|The boy hath ''sold'' him ''a bargain.'' {{right|''Shak.'', L. L. L., iii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|I see him ogle still, and hear him chat; ''Selling'' facetious ''bargains'', and propounding That witty recreation call’d dumfounding. {{right|''Dryden'', Prol. to Prophetess, l. 46.}}}} No maid at court is less asham’d, Howe’er for ''selling bargains'' fam’d. {{right|''Swift.''}} '''To strike a bargain''', {{smaller|to complete or ratify a bargain or an agreement, originally by ''striking'' or shaking hands.}} ='''Syn. 3.''' {{smaller|Covenant, mutual engagement.}} '''bargain''' (bär′gān), ''v.''   [< ME. ''bargainen'', ''bargaynen'', etc., < OF. ''bargaigner'' (F. ''barguigner'') = Pr. Pg. ''barganhar'' = It. ''bargagnare'', < ML. ''barcaniare'', traffic, trade, < *''barcania'', traffic: see the noun.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To treat about a transaction; make terms. {{smaller block|The thrifty state will ''bargain'' ere they fight. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}} '''2.''' To come to or make an agreement; stipulate; make or strike a bargain: ''with'' a person, ''for'' an object: as, he ''bargained with'' the producers ''for'' a daily supply. {{smaller block|So worthless peasants ''bargain for'' their wives As market-men ''for'' oxen, sheep, or horse. {{right|''Shak.'', 1 Hen. VI., v. 5.}} I alighted, and having ''bargained with'' my host ''for'' 20 crownes a moneth, I caused a good fire to be made in my chamber. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Nov. 4, 1644.}}}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To arrange beforehand by negotiation and agreement. {{smaller block|’Tis ''bargain’d'' . . . That she shall still be curst in company. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of the S., ii. 1.}}}} '''2†.''' To agree to buy or sell.—'''To bargain away''', {{smaller|to part with or lose as the result of a bargain.}} {{smaller block|The heir . . . had somehow ''bargained away'' the estate. {{right|''George Eliot'', Felix Holt, Int.}}}} '''bargain-chop''' (bär′gān-chop), ''n.'' A kind of gambling “option” on opium to arrive, formerly common among foreign traders in China.
